Variants.Content: Vaes Diaf is located on the Dothraki Sea inland of Essos, politically within the steppe world of Dothraki khalasars. It is a town, a center where surrounding populations, markets, roads and local power converge. Walls and roads tied the surrounding population, storage, and garrison here; even if the flags were changed, this stronghold would still affect how nearby people paid taxes, traded, and sought refuge.

How a stronghold falls on the people, in Westilfo, it starts with well water, stalls, food prices, wages and roads to the market. Local families also relied on pastures, horses, river branches, migration routes, and tribute from distant towns; if any road, well, spring, or wharf failed, the price would fall first on them.
Any military discussion about Westilf will eventually return to the city gates, streets, granaries, garrison numbers, and exits for evacuating the people. Entry Vaes Diaf

When the caravan writes Westilf into its account book, it will calculate the market day, warehouse rent, customs duties, coin quality and distance to neighboring cities. They also recognize the accents, laws, and credentials of the Dothraki Sea; reputations can travel great distances from taverns, and true distances must still be measured by wheel, oar, or horse's hoof.
Entry Vaes Diaf Entry Vaes Diaf

When veterans talk about Westilf, they rarely praise the scenery. They only remind others of the inn, stables, wells and whether they can still enter the city before nightfall. If you can supply supplies, avoid danger, and find a guide, it is worth marking in your itinerary; if you don't have these three things, no matter how loud your family name is, it won't be able to save the lost.

From the workshop to the sanctuary, Vesdelph juxtaposes the workshops, markets, roof tiles, church bells and the streets that have expanded through the ages with the fears and legends left by the horse god, the starry sky and the khalasars. A stronghold was therefore not just a lord's hall, but also a place where weddings and funerals, vows, labor and local memories recurred.

Entry Vaes Diaf They care about pastures, herds of horses, river branches, migration routes, and tributes from distant towns. They also look at whether seeds are left after harvesting grain, and whether city gates are open in times of disaster. When people from afar see coats of arms, what they see is whether there will be food to eat tomorrow.
